functions.doc:
Warnings and errors always show. An info notice is quiet by default, as roster's own routine messages are (`ui.messages`, like Neovim's): unless `ui.messages = "all"`, it isn't drawn, a screen reader still hears it and `:messages` keeps it. An info notice with buttons shows, and `quiet` decides either way: mark `quiet = false` on what the user asked for: the result of something they started ("Scan done: 12 Hosts answered, 3 new"), an answer ("No alerts") or a refusal ("Keep a Host first"), and leave it out for a routine confirmation ("Copied the line"). A quiet notice from a timer, an event or a request's answer, which the user didn't ask for, leaves a message line that shows something (an error, an answer) as it is. Every notice, shown or quiet, is in `:messages`.

A notice's button runs a command line when the user clicks it, as [`roster.cmd`](#rostercmdline) would: the click is the user's call, so `view ID` opens your view when a job that ran in the background has finished (a Plugin can't open one on its own, from a timer or an answer). It takes a command line, not a function, so a notice never holds on to one.

roster.notify("Plan ready: 4 Hosts change", "info", { actions = { { label = "Show the plan", run = "view mesh-plan" } } })
roster.notify("Scan done: 12 Hosts found", "info", { quiet = false })

  end)
  return "later"
end

lua_doc:
roster embeds **Lua 5.4** (built into the app, nothing to install), not LuaJIT as Neovim does; [why](adr/0006-lua-plugins-and-packages.md#why-lua-54-not-luajit). Coming from Neovim:

- Integers are real 64-bit integers (`3 // 2` is `1`, `math.type(1)` is `"integer"`), and the bitwise operators are native (`a & b`, `a | b`, `~a`, `a << 2`): there's no `bit` library.
- `goto`, `<const>` and `<close>` locals work; there's no `jit` and no FFI.
- The API is `roster.*`, never `vim.*`: there's no `vim.api`, `vim.fn`, `vim.loop` or `vim.schedule`.
- It runs in the [sandbox](app/config.md#the-sandbox): the base functions, `string`, `table`, `math`, `utf8` and an `os` with only `time`, `clock`, `date` and `difftime`. `coroutine` too (since api 3: a coroutine runs within the same time budget and memory limit). No `io`, no `os.execute`, no `debug`, no `package` and no C modules; `load` takes text only, and `require` loads only from the Plugin's own folder (`name.lua`, `name/init.lua`, or the same under `lua/`).
- `pairs` visits a table's keys in order: numbers, then text, then the rest. So the same state always makes the same changes in the same order, on every machine; `next` is Lua's own.
- An empty table is `{}` to the app, whether you meant a list or a table of fields: the app takes `{}` as an empty list wherever it wants one (`rows = {}`, `items = {}`).
- It runs on a thread of its own with a memory limit and a time budget per call: see [Limits](plugins.md#limits).

modules.doc: Every Plugin has a data folder of its own, in the app's data folder (next to the State; never the config folder, never on the network), and `roster.storage` reads and writes files there by name (decision Q93). No permission: it's the Plugin's own, and nothing else is reachable through it. A name is a plain file name (letters, digits, `-`, `_` and `.`, not starting with `.`; at most 100 characters), never a path, so there's no way out of the folder; a link there (a symlink, or a junction on Windows) is never followed. A write replaces the whole file at once (a temporary file, then a rename), so a crash leaves the old file or the new one, never half of one. A file holds at most 1 MB, the folder 10 MB in at most 1,000 files. The folder goes when the Plugin is removed (`:plugins remove`, or `:packages clean` for a Package), and stays across reloads, updates and revoked permissions. The time the disk takes doesn't count against the Plugin's budget.

modules.doc: `nil` unless the Plugin was granted at least one `network:<site>` permission ([Permissions](plugins.md#permissions)). The request runs in roster's core, never in the app's window, and doesn't wait: the function you pass gets the answer later, as a call of its own with a call's budget. Only the sites granted are reached, redirects included; a name that resolves to an address on this computer or a private network is refused unless the manifest lists the address itself, or the name as a private site (`network:private:nas.lan`), which reaches only private addresses. A pinned site (`#sha256:…`) trusts only that certificate. No cookies or credentials of roster's go along, and no proxy but the user's `plugin_proxy`, through which a public name is still looked up here first, refused if it leads inside, and reached only at the address roster checked (the proxy is asked for a tunnel to that address, never the name; a name this computer can't look up isn't sent). At most 4 requests at once, a 256 KB body out, a 1 MB body back, 30 seconds each.

Graph.doc: The app lays it out (each cluster's nodes on a spiral, the clusters in rows, loose nodes first), keeps every position in the State so it opens the same way each time, and draws only what's on screen, so 2,000 nodes stay smooth. Clusters collapse to one node with their count: the user's `o`, or by themselves when the graph has more than 300 nodes and the cluster doesn't say. Keys, once it has focus: `h` `j` `k` `l` or the arrows go to the nearest node that way, `/` searches (name, id, kind, note, detail, cluster; it opens empty each time) and `n`/`N` go through the matches, `Enter` runs `open` (or opens a collapsed cluster), `o` collapses or opens the selected node's cluster and `O` all of them, `+` `-` zoom and `0` shows it all, `H` `J` `K` `L` pan, `t` switches to a table of every node, then of every edge, `f` goes to the filter (the clusters, kinds and states to show, as many of each as the user ticks, hiding the rest; `Esc` clears a search, then the filter, then closes the view), `m` moves the selected node with `h` `j` `k` `l` or the arrows (`Shift` for a bigger step) until `Enter` keeps its place or `Esc` puts it back (on a collapsed cluster it says to open it first), and an action's `key` runs it on the selected node (only where its `when` matches). Selecting a node lights up what it can reach and what can reach it, with the counts: however many hops away, or only one with `reach = "direct"`. Hiding nodes doesn't change what they reach: the counts are the whole graph's. A click selects, a double click opens, a drag moves a node (kept) or pans, the wheel zooms. An edge whose end names nothing is left out until it does.
